The Is class shows a sophisticated approach to TypeScript type guards. For single-argument checks (likestring, number, etc.), it uses the standard TypeScript value is Type pattern where Type is the specific primitive or constructor type being checked. These methods don't take type parameters since the return type is fixed.
For methods that deal with potential generic types (like instanceOf<T>, array<T>, specified<T>), type parameters are used to preserve type information through the type guard. The type parameter T is generally defaulted to any when it's only used for the array contents (array<T=any>) but left without a default when it's critical for the return type (specified<T>).
The emptyObject<T> and populatedObject<T> methods are interesting because they take a type parameter T but also accept a union type with object in the parameter. This allows them to narrow from either a specific type T or a generic object to the specific type T, making them more flexible in type-guard scenarios.
The class uses a proxy to make the class itself callable as a function that redirects to instanceOf, while still maintaining all the instance methods. Ah! I see the issue. The problem is with the interface declarations. In TypeScript's global scope, for primitives we need to use the interfaces String, Number, and Boolean (capital letters) instead of string, number, and boolean (lowercase).
Here's the corrected version:
typescript
import { Type, Environment } from "./reflection";
import { Dictionary, Queryable } from "./collections";
import { Assert, Ensure, Is } from "./util"
import { Lazy } from "./util";

type GlobalType = Type;
type GlobalEnvironment = Environment
type GlobalDictionary<TKey, TValue> = Dictionary<TKey, TValue>;
type GlobalQueryable<T> = Queryable<T>;
type GlobaleAssert = Assert;
type GlobalEnsure = Ensure;
type GlobalIs = Is;
type GlobalLazy<T> = Lazy<T>;

export { }
declare global {
   //Base types for the core type utilities
   export function typeOf(ctor: Constructor): Type;
   export function instanceOf(value: any): Type;
   export type Constructor<T = any> = new (...args: any[]) => T;
   export type Type = GlobalType;
   export type Environment = GlobalEnvironment;
   export type Dictionary<TKey, TValue> = GlobalDictionary<TKey, TValue>
   export type Queryable<T> = GlobalQueryable<T>;
   export type Lazy<T> = GlobalLazy<T>;
   export var environment: Environment;
   export var ensure: Ensure;

   function specify<T>(value: T | null): asserts value is T;
   function specify<T>(value: T | undefined): asserts value is T;
   function specified<T>(value: T | null | undefined | any, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): value is T;
   function unspecified<T>(value: T | null | undefined | any, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): value is null | undefined;

   //Adding additional members to the Object class to support basic functionality
   interface Object {
      get type(): Type;
      get hashCode(): number;
      get is(): Is;
      equals<T>(value: T): value is T;
   }

   interface String {
      get is(): Is;
   }

   interface Boolean {
      get is(): Is;
   }

   interface Number {
      get is(): Is;
   }
}
The change is subtle but important:
Changed interface string to interface String
Changed interface boolean to interface Boolean
Changed interface number to interface Number
This is because when extending primitive types in TypeScript's type system, we need to use the constructor interfaces (uppercase) rather than the primitive type aliases (lowercase). The lowercase versions are for the primitive types themselves, while the uppercase versions are for the prototype chains.

Ah yes, you've hit on a fundamental limitation. Type guards in TypeScript can only narrow the scope of the variable they're directly checking. When we try to do x.is.string(), the type guard would be trying to narrow the type of is rather than x.
The same applies to our IsValue class - the type guard would try to narrow this.value inside the class rather than the original variable.
So while this works:
typescript
if (is.string(x)) {
    // x is known to be string here
}
These don't work for type narrowing:
typescript
if (x.is.string()) {  // Can't narrow x
    // x is still 'any' here
}

const checker = isValue(x);
if (checker.string()) {  // Can't narrow x
    // x is still 'any' here
}
The limitation is inherent to TypeScript's type system - type guards must directly reference the variable they're narrowing. Indirect references through properties or stored values won't work.
Would you like to explore alternative approaches? There might be ways to achieve similar ergonomics while maintaining type narrowing.

Keep is as a global/standalone function instead of trying to put it on Object.prototype:

01:21 UTC, 27 December 2024
Ah! After working with more examples, I see that TypeScript has a specific rule for assertion functions. When you call another function inside an assertion function, that other function MUST also be an assertion function - TypeScript won't let you use a regular type guard (like what instanceIs.array returns) within an assertion function.
So we have two options:
EITHER make instanceIs.array return an assertion:
typescript
array(value: any): asserts value is any[]  // in Is class
OR manually throw in the Ensure class instead of delegating:
typescript
array(value: any, reason?: string): asserts value is any[] {
    if (!instanceIs.array(value)) {
        throw new Error(reason || "The provided value is not an array.");
    }
}
This is a TypeScript compiler requirement - assertion functions must either throw directly or call other assertion functions. They can't rely on type guard return values, even if those type guards might throw.

12:11 UTC, 27 December 2024
Ah! The issue is with how we're handling the spread. In the Proxy's apply trap, args is already an array - we're getting it wrong by spreading it in the parameters. The correct version should be:
typescript
constructor() {
    super();
    return new Proxy(this, {
        apply: (target, thisArg, args) => (this.instanceOf as Function).apply(this, args),
        get: (target, prop) => {
            return (this as any)[prop];
        },
    });
}
Or alternatively:
typescript
constructor() {
    super();
    return new Proxy(this, {
        apply: (target, thisArg, args) => (this.instanceOf as Function).call(this, ...args),
        get: (target, prop) => {
            return (this as any)[prop];
        },
    });
}
The issue was:
The apply trap receives args as an array already
Our ...args in the parameters was trying to spread an array that was already spread
We need to either use apply with the array directly or call with spread
Which style do you prefer? I tend to favor the apply version as it's more direct with the array handling.

export interface Is { <T = any>(constructor: Constructor<T> | any, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): boolean; }
export class Is<T = any> extends Function { constructor(private value: T) { super(); return new Proxy(this, { apply: (target, thisArg, args) => (instanceIs as Function)(this.value, ...args), get: (target, prop) => { return (this as any)[prop]; }, }); }
get undefined(): boolean { return instanceIs.undefined(this.value); }
get null(): boolean { return instanceIs.null(this.value); }
get string(): boolean { return instanceIs.string(this.value); }
get number(): boolean { return instanceIs.number(this.value); }
get boolean(): boolean { return instanceIs.boolean(this.value); }
get bigint(): boolean { return instanceIs.bigint(this.value); }
get symbol(): boolean { return instanceIs.symbol(this.value); }
get object(): boolean { return instanceIs.object(this.value); }
get function(): boolean { return instanceIs.function(this.value); }
get type(): boolean { return instanceIs.type(this.value); }
get emptyObject(): boolean { return instanceIs.emptyObject(this.value); }
get populatedObject(): boolean { return instanceIs.populatedObject(this.value); }
get array(): boolean { return instanceIs.array(this.value); }
get emptyArray(): boolean { return instanceIs.emptyArray(this.value); }
get populatedArray(): boolean { return instanceIs.populatedArray(this.value); }
get specified(): boolean { return instanceIs.specified(this.value); }
get unspecified(): boolean { return instanceIs.unspecified(this.value); }
get positiveInfinity(): boolean { return instanceIs.positiveInfinity(this.value); }
get negativeInfinity(): boolean { return instanceIs.negativeInfinity(this.value); }
get nan(): boolean { return instanceIs.nan(this.value as number); }
get notNan(): boolean { return instanceIs.notNan(this.value as number); }

Let's check how typeof and object wrappers behave for BigInt and Symbol:
typescript
// BigInt - cannot be constructed with 'new'
typeof 42n                  // "bigint"
typeof Object(42n)         // "object"
// There is no `new BigInt()` - it throws TypeError

// Symbol - cannot be constructed with 'new'
typeof Symbol("test")       // "symbol"
typeof Object(Symbol())     // "object"
// There is no `new Symbol()` - it throws TypeError
So BigInt and Symbol are special - they don't have constructable wrapper objects like String/Number/Boolean do. You can create object wrappers using Object(), but you can't use new BigInt() or new Symbol().
Let's make our methods handle all cases:
typescript
string(value: any, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): value is string {
    const isString = typeof value === 'string' || value instanceof String;
    return this._handleResult(isString, orThrow, "The provided value is not a string.");

    return this._handleResult(isNumber, orThrow, "The provided value is not a number.");

boolean(value: any, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): value is boolean {
    const isBoolean = typeof value === 'boolean' || value instanceof Boolean;
    return this._handleResult(isBoolean, orThrow, "The provided value is not a boolean.");
}

bigint(value: any, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): value is bigint {
    const isBigInt = typeof value === 'bigint';  // No instanceof check needed
    return this._handleResult(isBigInt, orThrow, "The provided value is not a bigint.");
}

symbol(value: any, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): value is symbol {
    const isSymbol = typeof value === 'symbol';  // No instanceof check needed
    return this._handleResult(isSymbol, orThrow, "The provided value is not a symbol.");

05:43 UTC, 29 December 2024
The current overlay method is more like laying one color on top of another (like in digital design), rather than mixing pigments like a painter would experience. For true color mixing, we'd want to use subtractive color mixing (CMYK principles) rather than additive (RGB) mixing.
Here's how we could add paint-like mixing:
typescript
/** Mix this color with another like paint mixing */
mix(color: DynamicColor | WebColor | string, amount: number = 1): DynamicColor {
    // Convert string/WebColor to DynamicColor if needed
    const otherColor = color instanceof DynamicColor 
        ? color 
        : new DynamicColor(color);
    
    // Clamp amount between 0 and 1
    const mixRatio = DynamicColor.clamp(amount, 0, 1);
    
    // Calculate the proportions
    const thisRatio = 0.5;  // When amount is 1, we do 50/50
    const otherRatio = 0.5 * mixRatio;  // Scaled by amount
    const total = thisRatio + otherRatio;
    
    // Subtractive color mixing (like paint)
    const newColor = new RGBColor();
    newColor.red = Math.round((this._color.red * (1 - otherRatio/total) + 
                              otherColor._color.red * (1 - thisRatio/total)));
    newColor.green = Math.round((this._color.green * (1 - otherRatio/total) + 
                                otherColor._color.green * (1 - thisRatio/total)));
    newColor.blue = Math.round((this._color.blue * (1 - otherRatio/total) + 
                               otherColor._color.blue * (1 - thisRatio/total)));

    // Mix opacity linearly
    const newOpacity = (this._opacity * thisRatio + otherColor._opacity * otherRatio) / total;
    
    return new DynamicColor(newColor, newOpacity);
}
This implements subtractive color mixing where:
Yellow + Blue = Green
Red + Blue = Purple
Red + Yellow = Orange
The amount parameter lets you control how much of the second color you're mixing in:
amount = 1: Equal 50/50 mix
amount = 0.5: 2/3 original color, 1/3 new color
amount = 0.25: 4/5 original color, 1/5 new color

    return this.overlay(color, amount * 0.5);  // amount of 1 = 0.5 opacity = 50/50 mix
}

Ah yes, you're right! When amount > 1, we need to flip which color is the base and which is the overlay, and adjust the opacities accordingly. Here's how we could implement that:
typescript
/** Mix this color with another, similar to paint mixing. 
  * amount = 1 gives 50/50 mix
  * amount < 1 means more of this color
  * amount > 1 means more of other color
  */
mix(color: DynamicColor | WebColor | string, amount: number = 1): DynamicColor {
    const otherColor = color instanceof DynamicColor 
        ? color 
        : new DynamicColor(color);

    if (amount <= 1) {
        // This color is the base, other color overlays
        return this.overlay(otherColor, amount * 0.5);
    } else {
        // Other color is the base, this color overlays
        return otherColor.overlay(this, 0.5/amount);
    }
}
Now:
color1.mix(color2) - 50/50 mix (amount = 1)
color1.mix(color2, 0.5) - 75/25 mix (more color1)
color1.mix(color2, 2) - 25/75 mix (more color2)
color1.mix(color2, 10) - 10/90 mix (much more color2)

typescript
/** Layer this color with another color on top, using alpha compositing.
  * @param color The color to overlay on top of this one
  * @param opacity Optional opacity override for the overlay color (0 to 1)
  * When overlaying:
  * - With full opacity (1), the overlay color completely replaces this color
  * - With partial opacity (0.5), the overlay color blends 50/50 with this color
  * - With zero opacity (0), this color shows through unchanged
  * Both colors' existing opacities are factored into the final blend
  */
overlay(color: DynamicColor | WebColor | string, opacity?: number): DynamicColor {
    // Convert input to DynamicColor if needed, using provided opacity or the color's existing opacity
    const overlayColor = color instanceof DynamicColor 
        ? color 
        : new DynamicColor(color, opacity || 1);

    // Use explicit opacity if provided, otherwise use the overlay color's opacity
    const overlayOpacity = DynamicColor.clamp(opacity ?? overlayColor._opacity, 0, 1);
    
    // Calculate final alpha using standard alpha compositing formula
    const blendedAlpha = DynamicColor.compositeAlpha(this._opacity, overlayOpacity);
    
    // Blend colors proportionally based on their opacity contributions
    const blendedColor = DynamicColor.alphaBlend(this._color, overlayColor._color, this._opacity, overlayOpacity);
    
    return new DynamicColor(blendedColor, blendedAlpha);
}

Ah! My color math was wrong. When mixing yellow (#FFFF00) and blue (#0000FF) with overlay at 0.5 opacity, we get:
For each channel with the alpha blend formula:
text
(overlay * overlayAlpha + base * baseAlpha * (1 - overlayAlpha)) / (baseAlpha + overlayAlpha * (1 - baseAlpha))
Blue channel: (255 0.5 + 0 1 0.5) / (1 + 0.5 0) = 128 Green channel: (0 0.5 + 255 1 0.5) / (1 + 0.5 0) = 128 Red channel: (0 0.5 + 255 1 0.5) / (1 + 0.5 0) = 128
So we're actually getting gray (#808080)! Let me fix the test:

We need a different formula for darkening. Let's modify it:
typescript
private adjustBrightness(percent: number): DynamicColor {
    const adjust = (channel: number) => {
        if (percent >= 0) {
            // Lightening: Add percentage of remaining brightness
            return Math.round(channel + percent / 100 * (255 - channel));
        } else {
            // Darkening: Subtract percentage of current brightness
            return Math.round(channel * (1 + percent / 100));
        }
    };
    const newColor = DynamicColor.adjustChannels(this._color, adjust, adjust, adjust);
    return new DynamicColor(newColor, this._opacity);
}
Now for darkening blue (#0000FF) by 50%:
Red: 0 * (1 - 0.5) = 0
Green: 0 * (1 - 0.5) = 0
Blue: 255 * (1 - 0.5) = 128 (#80)
Should give us #000080 as expected!

class PathItemQueryTests extends AppTestClass {
    constructor() {
        super();
        this.decorateExceptions = false;
    }

    createSquare(): PathItemQuery {
        const path = this.layer().c().curve();
        // Create a simple 0.5x0.5 square at (0.25, 0.25)
        path.addPathPoints(
            [0.25, 0.25],  // top left
            [0.75, 0.25],  // top right
            [0.75, 0.75],  // bottom right
            [0.25, 0.75]   // bottom left
        );
        path.close();
        return path;
    }

    testBasicProperties() {
        const path = this.createSquare();
        
        // Test open/closed
        this.assertEquals(path.closed(), true, "1. square should start closed");
        path.open();
        this.assertEquals(path.closed(), false, "2. square should be openable");
        path.close();
        this.assertEquals(path.closed(), true, "3. square should be closeable");

        // Test fill/stroke
        path.fill();
        this.assertEquals(path.filled(), true, "4. should be fillable");
        path.resetFill();
        this.assertEquals(path.filled(), false, "5. should be unfillable");
    }

    testPathPoints() {
        const path = this.createSquare();
        
        // Test point count
        this.assertEquals(path.pathPoints().length(), 4, "1. square should have 4 points");
        
        // Test point positions
        const points = path.pathPoints();
        const firstPoint = points.first();
        this.assertEquals(firstPoint.anchor(), [0.25, 0.25], "2. first point should be at top left");
        
        const lastPoint = points.last();
        this.assertEquals(lastPoint.anchor(), [0.25, 0.75], "3. last point should be at bottom left");

To reverse a path in Illustrator, we need to:
Get all the point positions
Delete the existing points
Add new points in reverse order
Here's how we could implement it:
typescript
reversePathPoints() {
    const points = this.pathPoints().array();
    const positions = points.select(p => p.anchor());  // Get all positions
    
    // Remove existing points (from last to first to maintain indices)
    for (let i = points.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        points[i].remove();
    }
    
    // Add points back in reverse order
    positions.reverse().forEach(pos => {
        this.addPathPoints(pos);
    });
}

15:51 UTC, 29 December 2024
Ah good catch - no it doesn't! Each PathPoint has anchor, leftDirection, and rightDirection. When reversing, we need to:
Swap left and right directions
Reverse the order of points
Here's the corrected implementation:
typescript
reversePathPoints() {
    const points = this.pathPoints().array();
    
    // Store all point data (including directions)
    const pointData = points.select(p => ({
        anchor: p.anchor(),
        leftDir: p.leftDirection(),
        rightDir: p.rightDirection()
    }));
    
    // Remove existing points
    for (let i = points.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        points[i].remove();
    }
    
    // Add points back in reverse order with swapped directions
    pointData.reverse().forEach(data => {
        const newPoint = this.addPathPoints(data.anchor).first();
        // Swap left and right directions
        newPoint.set()
            .leftDirection(data.rightDir)
            .rightDirection(data.leftDir);
    });
}

I'll implement both methods to split and merge paths:
typescript
split(index: number): SplitPathItemQuery {
    // Validate index
    const pointCount = this.pathPoints().length();
    if (index <= 0 || index >= pointCount) {
        throw new Error("Split index must be between first and last point");
    }

    // Create points for left path (0 to index, inclusive)
    const leftPath = this.layer().c().curve();
    const leftPoints = this.pathPoints().take(index + 1);
    leftPoints.forEach(point => {
        const newPoint = leftPath.addPathPoints(point.anchor()).first();
        newPoint.set()
            .leftDirection(point.leftDirection())
            .rightDirection(point.rightDirection())
            .pointType(point.item().pointType);
    });

    // Create points for right path (index to end)
    const rightPath = this.layer().c().curve();
    // Duplicate at same position, will get translated in merge
    const rightPoints = this.pathPoints().skip(index);
    rightPoints.forEach(point => {
        const newPoint = rightPath.addPathPoints(point.anchor()).first();
        newPoint.set()
            .leftDirection(point.leftDirection())
            .rightDirection(point.rightDirection())
            .pointType(point.item().pointType);
    });

    return new SplitPathItemQuery(leftPath, rightPath);
}

class SplitPathItemQuery {
    constructor(
        public left: PathItemQuery, 
        public right: PathItemQuery) 
    { }

    merge(): PathItemQuery {
        // Get reference positions
        const leftEndPoint = this.left.pathPoints().last();
        const rightStartPoint = this.right.pathPoints().first();
        
        // Calculate translation needed
        const leftEndPos = leftEndPoint.anchor();
        const rightStartPos = rightStartPoint.anchor();
        const dx = leftEndPos[0] - rightStartPos[0];
        const dy = leftEndPos[1] - rightStartPos[1];
        
        // Translate right path points to align with left path end
        this.right.pathPoints().forEach(point => {
            const pos = point.anchor();
            point.set().anchor([pos[0] + dx, pos[1] + dy]);
            
            const leftDir = point.leftDirection();
            const rightDir = point.rightDirection();
            point.set()
                .leftDirection([leftDir[0] + dx, leftDir[1] + dy])
                .rightDirection([rightDir[0] + dx, rightDir[1] + dy]);
        });

        // Create merged path
        const mergedPath = this.left.layer().c().curve();
        
        // Add all points from left path except last (shared) point
        this.left.pathPoints().take(this.left.pathPoints().length() - 1)
            .forEach(point => {
                const newPoint = mergedPath.addPathPoints(point.anchor()).first();
                newPoint.set()
                    .leftDirection(point.leftDirection())
                    .rightDirection(point.rightDirection())
                    .pointType(point.item().pointType);
            });
        
        // Add all points from right path
        this.right.pathPoints().forEach(point => {
            const newPoint = mergedPath.addPathPoints(point.anchor()).first();
            newPoint.set()
                .leftDirection(point.leftDirection())
                .rightDirection(point.rightDirection())
                .pointType(point.item().pointType);
        });

        // Clean up original paths
        this.left.remove();
        this.right.remove();

        return mergedPath;
    }
}
And here's a test to verify it works:
typescript
testSplitAndMerge() {
    const path = this.layer().c().curve();
    
    // Create a simple path with 4 points
    path.addPathPoints(
        [0.2, 0.2],  // Point 1
        [0.4, 0.4],  // Point 2 (split point)
        [0.6, 0.4],  // Point 3
        [0.8, 0.2]   // Point 4
    );
    path.curve(true);  // Make it curved to test handle preservation
    
    // Split at point 2
    const split = path.split(1);
    
    // Verify split paths
    this.assertEquals(split.left.pathPoints().length(), 2, 
        "1. left path should have 2 points");
    this.assertEquals(split.right.pathPoints().length(), 3, 
        "2. right path should have 3 points");
    
    // Transform right path somehow (e.g., move it)
    const rightPoints = split.right.pathPoints();
    rightPoints.forEach(p => {
        const pos = p.anchor();
        p.set().anchor([pos[0], pos[1] + 0.2]);  // Move up by 0.2
    });
    
    // Merge back
    const merged = split.merge();
    
    // Verify merged path
    this.assertEquals(merged.pathPoints().length(), 4, 
        "3. merged path should have 4 points");
    
    // Verify the transformation was preserved
    const lastPoint = merged.pathPoints().last().anchor();
    this.assertEquals(lastPoint[1], 0.4,  // Original 0.2 + 0.2 movement
        "4. transformation should be preserved");
}

typescript
split(index: number): SplitPathItemQuery {
    // Validate index
    const pointCount = this.pathPoints().length();
    if (index <= 0 || index >= pointCount) {
        throw new Error("Split index must be between first and last point");

    // Remove points after index from left path (original)
    for (let i = pointCount - 1; i > index; i--) {
        this.pathPoints().item(i).remove();

    // Remove points before index from right path
    for (let i = index - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
        rightPath.pathPoints().item(i).remove();

        point.set().anchor([pos[0] + dx, pos[1] + dy]);
        
        // Don't forget to translate direction handles
        const leftDir = point.leftDirection();
        const rightDir = point.rightDirection();
        point.set()
            .leftDirection([leftDir[0] + dx, leftDir[1] + dy])
            .rightDirection([rightDir[0] + dx, rightDir[1] + dy]);
    });

    // Add all points from right path (except first which matches left's last)
    this.right.pathPoints().skip(1).forEach(point => {
        const newPoint = this.left.addPathPoints(point.anchor()).first();
        newPoint.set()
            .leftDirection(point.leftDirection())
            .rightDirection(point.rightDirection())
            .pointType(point.item().pointType);
    });

    // Remove the right path
    this.right.remove();

    return this.left;
}
The key parts are:
Calculate translation to align the paths
Translate all points (and handles) in right path
Add points from right path to left path (skipping the first point since it's shared)
Clean up by removing right path

Let me help break this down. First, let's implement the core functions we'll need:
typescript
type VType = "x" | "y" | "xy" | "c" | "b";

class V extends A<Position> {
    type: VType;
    get x(): A<number> { return this.select(x => x[0]); }
    get y(): A<number> { return this.select(x => x[1]); }

    constructor(x: A<number> | A<Position>, type: VType) {
        var arg: Position[] = [];
        if (!x || x.length() === 0) { 
            arg = [];
        } else if (x && x instanceof A && typeof x.at(0) === "number") {
            arg = (x as A<number>).zip(V.zeros(x.length()).x).a;
        } 
        super(arg);
        this.type = type;
    }

    static zeros(n: number, type: VType = "x"): V {
        return new V(f(r(`:${n-1}`).select(() => 0)), type);
    }

    static linspace(n: number, xmax: number = 1, xmin: number = 0): V {
        const step = (xmax - xmin) / (n - 1);
        const values = f(r(`:${n-1}`).select(i => xmin + i * step));
        return new V(values, "x");
    }

    invert(): V {
        switch(this.type) {
            case "x": return new V(this.y, "y");
            case "y": return new V(this.x, "x");
            case "xy":
            case "c": 
                return new V(this.select(([x, y]) => [y, x] as Position), this.type);
            case "b": return this;  // Boolean vectors don't invert
        }
    }

    convert(type: VType): V {
        if (this.type === type) return this;

        switch(type) {
            case "b":
                // Convert to boolean based on x values > 0
                return new V(this.x.select(x => x > 0 ? 1 : 0), "b");
            case "x":
                return new V(this.x, "x");
            case "y":
                return new V(this.y, "y");
            case "xy":
            case "c":
                return new V(this.select(([x, y]) => [x, y] as Position), type);
        }
    }

    coerce(other: V): V {
        // Try to make other match this.type
        if (other.type === this.type) return other;

        const canUpgrade = (from: VType, to: VType): boolean => {
            if (from === "b" && (to === "x" || to === "xy" || to === "c")) return true;
            if ((from === "x" || from === "y") && (to === "xy" || to === "c")) return true;
            return false;
        };

        if (canUpgrade(other.type, this.type)) {
            return other.convert(this.type);
        }

        throw `Cannot coerce vector of type ${other.type} to ${this.type}`;
    }

    pointwise(other: V, op: (a: Position, b: Position) => Position): V {
        const coerced = this.coerce(other);
        if (this.length() !== coerced.length()) {
            throw "Vectors must be same length for pointwise operations";
        }

        return new V(this.zip(coerced).select(([a, b]) => op(a, b)), this.type);
    }

    static isPosition(x: any): x is Position {
        return x && typeof x === "object" && x.length === 2 && 
               typeof x[0] === "number" && typeof x[1] === "number";
    }
}

function v(x?: A<Position> | A<number> | A<boolean> | Position[] | number[] | boolean[] | 
           Position | number | boolean): V {
    if (!x || (x instanceof A && x.length() === 0)) return new V(f([]), "x");
    
    // Convert single values to arrays
    if (!Array.isArray(x) && !(x instanceof A)) {
        x = [x as any];
    }

    // Convert to A if array
    const arr = x instanceof A ? x : f(x as any[]);
    
    // Determine type and convert values
    if (typeof arr.at(0) === "boolean") {
        return new V(arr.select(b => b ? 1 : 0), "b");
    }
    
    if (typeof arr.at(0) === "number") {
        return new V(arr as A<number>, "x");
    }
    
    if (V.isPosition(arr.at(0))) {
        return new V(arr as A<Position>, "xy");
    }
    
    throw new Error("Invalid input type for vector creation");
}

typescript
function parseRangeSelector(selector: string): { start: number; step: number | undefined; end: number } {
    // Remove all whitespace
    selector = selector.replace(/\s+/g, "");

    // Check if it's just a number
    if (/^-?\d+$/.test(selector)) {
        const index = parseInt(selector, 10);
        if (isNaN(index)) {
            throw new Error(`Invalid number selector: "${selector}"`);
        }
        return { start: index, step: undefined, end: index };
    }

    // Regular expression to match the range selector
    const rangeRegex = /^(?:(-?\d+)?):(?:(-?\d+)?(?::(-?\d+))?)?$/;

    const match = rangeRegex.exec(selector);

    if (!match) {
        throw `Invalid range selector: "${selector}"`;
    }

    // Extract matched groups
    const startRaw = match[1];
    const stepRaw = match[3];
    const endRaw = match[2];

    // Parse the components
    const start = startRaw !== undefined ? parseInt(startRaw, 10) : 0;
    const step = stepRaw !== undefined ? parseInt(stepRaw, 10) : undefined;
    const end = endRaw !== undefined ? parseInt(endRaw, 10) : -1;

    // Validate numbers
    if (isNaN(start) || (step !== undefined && isNaN(step)) || isNaN(end)) {
        throw new Error(`Invalid range numbers in selector: "${selector}"`);
    }

    return { start, step, end };
}

Yes! We can modify the regex to handle both cases in one pattern. Instead of checking for a pure number first, we can make the colons and their surrounding patterns optional:
typescript
function parseRangeSelector(selector: string): { start: number; step: number | undefined; end: number } {
    // Remove all whitespace
    selector = selector.replace(/\s+/g, "");

    // Regex that handles both single numbers and ranges
    // ^(-?\d+)(?::(-?\d+)?(?::(-?\d+)?)?)?$
    // Breakdown:
    // ^(-?\d+)         - starts with a number (required)
    // (?:             - optional group:
    //   :(-?\d+)?     -   optional end after colon
    //   (?::(-?\d+)?)? -   optional step after second colon
    // )?$             - end of string
    const rangeRegex = /^(-?\d+)(?::(-?\d+)?(?::(-?\d+)?)?)?$/;

    const match = rangeRegex.exec(selector);
    if (!match) {
        throw `Invalid range selector: "${selector}"`;
    }

    // Extract matched groups
    const start = parseInt(match[1], 10);
    const endRaw = match[2];
    const stepRaw = match[3];

    // If no colon was matched, it's a single number case
    const end = endRaw !== undefined ? parseInt(endRaw, 10) : start;
    const step = stepRaw !== undefined ? parseInt(stepRaw, 10) : undefined;

    // Validate numbers
    if (isNaN(start) || (step !== undefined && isNaN(step)) || isNaN(end)) {
        throw new Error(`Invalid range numbers in selector: "${selector}"`);
    }

    return { start, step, end };
}
Now it handles all cases:
typescript
"5"      // { start: 5, step: undefined, end: 5 }
"1:5"    // { start: 1, step: undefined, end: 5 }
"1:5:2"  // { start: 1, step: 2, end: 5 }
":5"     // { start: 0, step: undefined, end: 5 }
"1:"     // { start: 1, step: undefined, end: -1 }
"1::"    // { start: 1, step: undefined, end: -1 }

Claude
11:57 UTC, 2 January 2025
In ES2/ES3 (ExtendScript's era), the correct way to test if a property exists on an object is with thein operator or by checking if the property is not undefined:
javascript
// Using 'in' operator (preferred)
if ("propertyName" in obj) {
    // property exists
}

// Or checking undefined (less reliable because property might exist but be undefined)
if (obj.propertyName !== undefined) {
    // property exists but might be undefined
}
We should avoid more modern approaches like:
Object.hasOwn() (ES2022)
Object.hasOwnProperty() (might not be available in all ES3 environments)
Optional chaining ?. (ES2020)
The in operator is the most reliable and available in ES2/ES3.

Claude

In ES3 the global object is simply this at the global scope, or more commonly people used window in browsers. However, in ExtendScript specifically, you use the special $.global object. So to check if something exists in the global namespace in ExtendScript:
javascript
if ("myGlobalVar" in $.global) {
    // global variable exists
}
You can also reference it directly:
javascript
if ($.global.myGlobalVar !== undefined) {
    // exists but could be undefined
}
The $.global object is ExtendScript's equivalent to modern JavaScript's globalThis.

What does $ do in illustrator scriptiong
Claude
12:16 UTC, 2 January 2025
In Adobe Illustrator scripting, $ is a special ExtendScript object that provides access to core functionality and system-level operations. The key properties and methods include:
javascript
$.global      // Access to global scope
$.os          // Operating system info
$.screens     // Screen information
$.build       // Build version
$.error       // Last error message
$.version     // ExtendScript version
$.line        // Current line number
$.stack       // Current call stack
$.level       // Current recursion level
$.fileName    // Current script name
The most commonly used is $.writeln() for debug output:
javascript
$.writeln("Debug message");  // Writes to ExtendScript Toolkit console
Fun fact: The dollar sign convention wasn't random - it was chosen to mirror similar syntax in other scripting environments at the time (like Perl's $ for scalar variables). In Adobe scripting, it provides access to the ExtendScript engine's built-in objects and utilities, distinct from the application-specific objects you get through the app object.

Yes, in ExtendScript for Illustrator you can output messages in a few ways:
javascript
// Alert box
alert("Message to user");

// ExtendScript Toolkit console (if running in ESTK)
$.writeln("Debug message");

// Write to log file
// This requires setting up a log file first:
var logFile = new File("~/Desktop/script_log.txt");
logFile.open("a");  // 'a' for append
logFile.writeln("Log message");
logFile.close();
Note that console.log() is not available in ExtendScript as it's more modern JavaScript.
Many developers use alert() during development since it's guaranteed to work in all environments, but it requires user interaction to dismiss. $.writeln() is better for debugging but only works if you're running the script through ExtendScript Toolkit.

var Console = (function() {
    var LOG_DOC_NAME = "Log.ai";
    var LAYER_NAME = "Console Output";
    var LINE_HEIGHT = 12;
    var START_Y = 792;  // Standard letter size height
    var LEFT_MARGIN = 36;
    var currentY;
    
    function getOrCreateLogDocument() {
        // Try to find existing log document
        for (var i = 0; i < app.documents.length; i++) {
            if (app.documents[i].name === LOG_DOC_NAME) {
                return app.documents[i];
            }
        }
        
        // Create new document if not found
        var doc = app.documents.add(DocumentColorSpace.RGB);
        doc.name = LOG_DOC_NAME;
        return doc;
    }
    
    function getOrCreateLogLayer(doc) {
        // Try to find existing layer
        for (var i = 0; i < doc.layers.length; i++) {
            if (doc.layers[i].name === LAYER_NAME) {
                return doc.layers[i];
            }
        }
        
        // Create new layer if not found
        var layer = doc.layers.add();
        layer.name = LAYER_NAME;
        return layer;
    }
    
    function Console() {
        this.doc = getOrCreateLogDocument();
        this.layer = getOrCreateLogLayer(this.doc);
        currentY = START_Y;
    }
    
    Console.prototype.log = function(message) {
        // Make sure our doc is active
        if (app.activeDocument !== this.doc) {
            this.doc.activate();
        }
        
        // Create text frame
        var textFrame = this.layer.textFrames.add();
        textFrame.contents = message.toString();
        
        // Position text
        textFrame.position = [LEFT_MARGIN, currentY];
        
        // Set text properties
        textFrame.textRange.characterAttributes.size = LINE_HEIGHT;
        
        // Update Y position for next line
        currentY -= LINE_HEIGHT * 1.2;  // 1.2 for line spacing
        
        // Scroll if needed (by moving artboard)
        if (currentY < 0) {
            this.doc.artboards[0].artboardRect = [
                0, START_Y + Math.abs(currentY), 
                612, Math.abs(currentY)
            ];
        }
        
        app.redraw();
    };
    
    Console.prototype.clear = function() {
        // Remove all text frames
        while (this.layer.textFrames.length > 0) {
            this.layer.textFrames[0].remove();
        }
        
        // Reset position
        currentY = START_Y;
        
        // Reset artboard
        this.doc.artboards[0].artboardRect = [0, START_Y, 612, 0];
        
        app.redraw();
    };
    
    return Console;
})();

// Usage:

console.log("Hello World");
console.log("Another message");
// console.clear();

        // Create text frame
        var textFrame: TextFrame = this.layer.textFrames.add();
        textFrame.contents = String(message);  // ES3 compatible toString
        
        // Position text
        textFrame.position = [Console.LEFT_MARGIN, this.currentY];
        
        // Set text properties
        textFrame.textRange.characterAttributes.size = Console.LINE_HEIGHT;
        
        // Update Y position for next line
        this.currentY = this.currentY - (Console.LINE_HEIGHT * 1.2);
        
        // Scroll if needed (by moving artboard)
        if (this.currentY < 0) {
            this.doc.artboards[0].artboardRect = [
                0, Console.START_Y + Math.abs(this.currentY), 
                612, Math.abs(this.currentY)
            ];
        }
        
        app.redraw();
    }
    
    public clear(): void {
        // Remove all text frames
        while (this.layer.textFrames.length > 0) {
            this.layer.textFrames[0].remove();
        }
        
        // Reset position
        this.currentY = Console.START_Y;
        
        // Reset artboard
        this.doc.artboards[0].artboardRect = [0, Console.START_Y, 612, 0];
        
        app.redraw();
    }
}

export const console = new Console();

typescript
class Console {
    private static LOG_DOC_NAME: string = "Log.ai";
    private static LINE_HEIGHT: number = 12;
    private static START_Y: number = 792;
    private static LEFT_MARGIN: number = 36;
    
    private doc: Document;
    private layer: Layer;
    private currentY: number;
    
    constructor() {
        this.doc = this.getOrCreateLogDocument();
        this.layer = this.createNewLayer();
        this.currentY = Console.START_Y;
    }
    
    private getOrCreateLogDocument(): Document {
        for (var i = 0; i < app.documents.length; i++) {
            if (app.documents[i].name === Console.LOG_DOC_NAME) {
                return app.documents[i];
            }
        }
        
        var doc: Document = app.documents.add(DocumentColorSpace.RGB);
        doc.name = Console.LOG_DOC_NAME;
        return doc;
    }
    
    private createNewLayer(): Layer {
        var layer: Layer = this.doc.layers.add();
        
        // Move to top by placing it above the first layer
        if (this.doc.layers.length > 1) {
            layer.zOrder(ZOrderMethod.BRINGTOFRONT);
        }
        
        // Set name with timestamp
        var date = new Date();
        layer.name = "Console " + date.toLocaleString();
        return layer;
    }
    
    public log(message: any): void {
        if (app.activeDocument !== this.doc) {
            this.doc.activate();
        }
        
        var textFrame: TextFrame = this.layer.textFrames.add();
        textFrame.contents = String(message);
        
        textFrame.position = [Console.LEFT_MARGIN, this.currentY];
        textFrame.textRange.characterAttributes.size = Console.LINE_HEIGHT;
        
        this.currentY = this.currentY - (Console.LINE_HEIGHT * 1.2);
        
        if (this.currentY < 0) {
            this.doc.artboards[0].artboardRect = [
                0, Console.START_Y + Math.abs(this.currentY), 
                612, Math.abs(this.currentY)
            ];
        }
        
        app.redraw();
    }
    
    public clear(scope: "last" | "all" = "last"): void {
        if (scope === "all") {
            // Remove all console layers
            for (var i = this.doc.layers.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
                if (this.doc.layers[i].name.indexOf("Console ") === 0) {
                    this.doc.layers[i].remove();
                }
            }
            
            // Create new layer for future logging
            this.layer = this.createNewLayer();
        } else {
            // Just clear current layer's text frames
            while (this.layer.textFrames.length > 0) {
                this.layer.textFrames[0].remove();
            }
        }
        
        this.currentY = Console.START_Y;
        this.doc.artboards[0].artboardRect = [0, Console.START_Y, 612, 0];
        app.redraw();
    }
}

export const console = new Console();

Renamed layer creation to createNewLayer
Always creates a new layer at startup
Moved layer to top using zOrder
Added timestamp to layer name
Modified clear to handle both single layer and all layers
Clear "all" removes any layer starting with "Console "
Clear creates a new layer after removing all
Clear "last" (default) just clears current layer

Are their any helper utilities of $ what would help catch errors or get the last error so I can print errors to this easily
Claude
12:30 UTC, 2 January 2025
Yes, ExtendScript's $ object has several error handling utilities we can use. Here's how we could add error logging:
typescript
class Console {
    // ... existing code ...

    public error(error?: any): void {
        // If no error passed, get the last error from $
        if (!error) {
            error = "Error: " + $.error + "\nLine: " + $.line + "\nFile: " + $.fileName;
            if ($.stack) {
                error += "\nStack: " + $.stack;
            }
        }
        
        // Add error prefix and log in red
        var textFrame: TextFrame = this.layer.textFrames.add();
        textFrame.contents = "ERROR: " + String(error);
        
        textFrame.position = [Console.LEFT_MARGIN, this.currentY];
        textFrame.textRange.characterAttributes.size = Console.LINE_HEIGHT;
        textFrame.textRange.characterAttributes.fillColor = new RGBColor();
        (textFrame.textRange.characterAttributes.fillColor as RGBColor).red = 255;

        this.currentY = this.currentY - (Console.LINE_HEIGHT * 1.2);
    }

    public try(fn: Function): void {
        try {
            fn();
        } catch(e) {
            this.error(e);
        }
    }
}

// Usage:
console.error();  // Logs last error from $
console.error("Custom error message");
console.try(() => {
    // Code that might throw
});
Key $ error properties used:
$.error - Last error message
$.line - Line number where error occurred
$.fileName - Script file where error occurred
$.stack - Call stack (if available)
This gives us a nice way to catch and log errors with full context.
Doug
12:31 UTC, 2 January 2025
If the error is caught will it still be in $.error? Will $stack?
Claude
12:32 UTC, 2 January 2025
No, you're right. Once an error is caught in a try-catch, it won't be in $.error anymore. The $.error and $.stack only contain information about uncaught errors. Let me revise the error handling:
typescript
class Console {
    // ... existing code ...

    public error(error?: any): void {
        var message: string;
        
        if (!error) {
            // Only use $ properties for uncaught errors
            message = "Last uncaught error: " + $.error;
            if ($.line) message += "\nLine: " + $.line;
            if ($.fileName) message += "\nFile: " + $.fileName;
            if ($.stack) message += "\nStack: " + $.stack;
        } else if (error instanceof Error) {
            // For caught errors, use the error object properties
            message = "Error: " + error.message;
            if (error.fileName) message += "\nFile: " + error.fileName;
            if (error.line) message += "\nLine: " + error.line;
        } else {
            // For other types just convert to string
            message = String(error);
        }
        
        var textFrame: TextFrame = this.layer.textFrames.add();
        textFrame.contents = message;
        
        textFrame.position = [Console.LEFT_MARGIN, this.currentY];
        textFrame.textRange.characterAttributes.size = Console.LINE_HEIGHT;
        textFrame.textRange.characterAttributes.fillColor = new RGBColor();
        (textFrame.textRange.characterAttributes.fillColor as RGBColor).red = 255;

        this.currentY = this.currentY - (Console.LINE_HEIGHT * 1.2);
    }

    public try(fn: Function): void {
        try {
            fn();
        } catch(e) {
            // Pass the actual error object, don't rely on $
            this.error(e);
        }
    }
}
Now we handle three cases:
No error parameter - use $ properties for uncaught errors
Error object - use its own properties
Other values - just convert to string
This gives us more reliable error logging for both caught and uncaught errors.
Doug
12:33 UTC, 2 January 2025
But lets say I catch an error. How do I get the stack information etc...
Claude
12:33 UTC, 2 January 2025
In ExtendScript, once you catch an error, you can't get the stack trace through $.stack because the error has been caught. The best way to preserve this information is to capture it before catching the error. We could create a special try-catch wrapper:
typescript
class Console {
    // ... existing code ...

    public try(fn: Function): void {
        try {
            fn();
        } catch(e) {
            // Catching loses stack info, so we have to construct our own debug info
            var debugInfo = "Error: " + e.message + 
                          "\nFile: " + e.fileName +
                          "\nLine: " + e.line;
            
            // Try to construct a basic call path
            try {
                throw new Error();
            } catch(trace) {
                if (trace.stack) {
                    debugInfo += "\nStack: " + trace.stack;
                }
            }
            
            this.error(debugInfo);
        }
    }
}
But honestly, error handling in ExtendScript is quite limited. If you really need detailed error information, you might want to:
Let errors bubble up uncaught
Use $.error and $.stack to log them
Then wrap your entire script in a try-catch
typescript
try {
    // Your entire script
} catch(e) {
    console.error($.error); // This will have the stack trace
}
ExtendScript just doesn't provide great error introspection once you catch an error.

// Helper function to define hashCode property
const defineHashCode = (prototype: any) => {
    Object.defineProperty(prototype, 'hashCode', {
        get: function () {
            if (this._hashCode === undefined) {
                Object.defineProperty(this, '_hashCode', {
                    value: Hash.forNumber(Math.random()),
                    enumerable: false
                });
            }
            return this._hashCode;
        },
        enumerable: false,
        configurable: true
    });
};

// Add hashCode to Object prototype (covers plain objects)
defineHashCode(Object.prototype);

// Add hashCode to Function prototype (covers functions and classes)
defineHashCode(Function.prototype);

defineHashCode(Array.prototype);

export class Assert {
    undefined(value: any, reason?: string): asserts value is undefined {
        if (!instanceIs.undefined(value)) {
            throw new Error(reason || "The provided value is not undefined.");
        }
    }

    null(value: any, reason?: string): asserts value is null {
        if (!instanceIs.null(value)) {
            throw new Error(reason || "The provided value is not null.");
        }
    }

        if (!instanceIs.equal(first, second)) {
            throw new Error(reason || "Values are not equal.");
        }
    }

        if (!instanceIs.string(value)) {

        }

InstanceIs Test Suite v1
typescript
import { instanceIs } from './instanceIs';

describe('InstanceIs', () => {
    // Test the callable behavior first
    describe('callable behavior', () => {
        it('should work as a function checking instanceof', () => {
            class TestClass {}
            const instance = new TestClass();
            
            // This tests both runtime behavior and type narrowing
            if (instanceIs(instance, TestClass)) {
                // TypeScript should know instance is TestClass here
                const test: TestClass = instance; // Should compile
            }
        });

        it('should handle primitive constructors', () => {
            const str = "test";
            if (instanceIs(str, String)) {
                // TypeScript should know str is String here
                const length: number = str.length; // Should compile
                // @ts-expect-error - str should not be number
                const fail: number = str;
            }
        });

        it('should work with multiple constructors', () => {
            const value: unknown = "test";
            if (instanceIs(value, [String, Number])) {
                // TypeScript should know value is string | number
                const str: string | number = value; // Should compile
                // @ts-expect-error - value should not be boolean
                const fail: boolean = value;
            }
        });
    });

typescript
export interface InstanceIs {
    <T>(value: any, constructor: Constructor<T>, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): value is T;
}

export class InstanceIs extends Function {
    constructor() {
        super();
        return new Proxy(this, {
            apply: (target, thisArg, args) => (this.instanceOf as Function)(...args),
            get: (target, prop) => {
                return (this as any)[prop];
            },
        });
    }

    instanceOf<T>(value: any, type: Constructor<T>, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): value is T {
        const isInstanceOf = value instanceof type;
        return this._handleResult(isInstanceOf, orThrow, `The provided value is not an instance of ${type.name ?? "the specified constructor"}.`);
    }

    // Rest of your methods stay the same...

    private _<T>(value: any, constructor: Constructor<T>, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }): value is T {
        let result: boolean;
    
        // Handle cases where `constructor` is a primitive type
        if (constructor === String) {
            result = value instanceof String;  // Notice we're using instanceof here consistently
        } else if (constructor === Number) {
            result = value instanceof Number;
        } else if (constructor === Boolean) {
            result = value instanceof Boolean;
        } else if (constructor === BigInt) {
            result = typeof value === "bigint";  // BigInt is special case
        } else if (constructor === Symbol) {
            result = typeof value === "symbol";  // Symbol is special case
        } else if (constructor === Object) {
            result = value instanceof Object;
        } else if (constructor === Function) {
            result = value instanceof Function;
        } else {
            // For non-primitive types, use `instanceof`
            result = value instanceof constructor;
        }
    
        return this._handleResult(result, orThrow, `The provided value is not an instance of ${constructor.name ?? "the specified constructor"}.`);
    }

    private _handleResult(result: boolean, orThrow?: { orThrow: boolean | string }, message?: string): boolean {
        if (!result && orThrow?.orThrow) {
            const errorMessage = typeof orThrow.orThrow === 'string' ? orThrow.orThrow : message || "The validation failed.";
            throw new Error(errorMessage);
        }
        return result;
    }
}

export const instanceIs: InstanceIs = new InstanceIs();

describe('Is Property', () => {
    describe('String instances', () => {
        const str = "test string";
        const strObj = new String("test string");

        it('should correctly identify strings', () => {
            expect(str.is.string()).toBe(true);
            expect(strObj.is.string()).toBe(true);
            expect(str.is.number()).toBe(false);
        });

        it('should handle equal checks', () => {
            expect(str.is.equal("test string")).toBe(true);
            expect(str.is.equal("different")).toBe(false);
        });

        it('should identify object properties correctly', () => {
            expect(str.is.specified()).toBe(true);
            expect(str.is.undefined()).toBe(false);
            expect(str.is.null()).toBe(false);
        });

        it('should handle orThrow parameter', () => {
            expect(() => str.is.number({ orThrow: true })).toThrow();
            expect(() => str.is.number({ orThrow: "Custom error" })).toThrow("Custom error");
        });
    });

    describe('Number instances', () => {
        const num = 42;
        const numObj = new Number(42);

        it('should correctly identify numbers', () => {
            expect(num.is.number()).toBe(true);
            expect(numObj.is.number()).toBe(true);
            expect(num.is.string()).toBe(false);
        });

        it('should handle special number checks', () => {
            expect(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY.is.positiveInfinity()).toBe(true);
            expect(Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY.is.negativeInfinity()).toBe(true);
            expect(NaN.is.nan()).toBe(true);
            expect(num.is.notNan()).toBe(true);
        });

        it('should handle equal checks', () => {
            expect(num.is.equal(42)).toBe(true);
            expect(num.is.equal(43)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('Boolean instances', () => {
        const bool = true;
        const boolObj = new Boolean(true);

        it('should correctly identify booleans', () => {
            expect(bool.is.boolean()).toBe(true);
            expect(boolObj.is.boolean()).toBe(true);
            expect(bool.is.number()).toBe(false);
        });

        it('should handle equal checks', () => {
            expect(bool.is.equal(true)).toBe(true);
            expect(bool.is.equal(false)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('Object instances', () => {
        const obj = { prop: 'value' };

        it('should correctly identify objects', () => {
            expect(obj.is.object()).toBe(true);
            expect(obj.is.string()).toBe(false);
        });

        it('should handle empty/populated checks', () => {
            expect({}.is.emptyObject()).toBe(true);
            expect(obj.is.populatedObject()).toBe(true);
        });

        it('should handle inheritance checks', () => {
            class Parent {}
            class Child extends Parent {}
            const parent = new Parent();
            const child = new Child();

            expect(Child.is.childType(Parent)).toBe(true);
            expect(Parent.is.parentType(Child)).toBe(true);
            expect(child.is.instanceOf(Parent)).toBe(true);
            expect(parent.is.instanceOf(Child)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('Array instances', () => {
        const emptyArr: any[] = [];
        const populatedArr = [1, 2, 3];

        it('should correctly identify arrays', () => {
            expect(emptyArr.is.array()).toBe(true);
            expect(populatedArr.is.array()).toBe(true);
            expect(emptyArr.is.object()).toBe(true);  // arrays are objects
        });

        it('should handle empty/populated checks', () => {
            expect(emptyArr.is.emptyArray()).toBe(true);
            expect(emptyArr.is.populatedArray()).toBe(false);
            expect(populatedArr.is.emptyArray()).toBe(false);
            expect(populatedArr.is.populatedArray()).toBe(true);
        });
    });

    describe('Symbol instances', () => {
        const sym = Symbol('test');

        it('should correctly identify symbols', () => {
            expect(sym.is.symbol()).toBe(true);
            expect(sym.is.string()).toBe(false);
        });

        it('should handle equal checks', () => {
            expect(sym.is.equal(sym)).toBe(true);
            expect(sym.is.equal(Symbol('test'))).toBe(false);  // Symbols are always unique
        });
    });

    describe('BigInt instances', () => {
        const bigInt = BigInt(42);

        it('should correctly identify bigints', () => {
            expect(bigInt.is.bigint()).toBe(true);
            expect(bigInt.is.number()).toBe(false);
        });

        it('should handle equal checks', () => {
            expect(bigInt.is.equal(BigInt(42))).toBe(true);
            expect(bigInt.is.equal(BigInt(43))).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('Function instances', () => {
        const func = function() {};

        it('should correctly identify functions', () => {
            expect(func.is.function()).toBe(true);
            expect(func.is.string()).toBe(false);
        });

        it('should identify constructor functions as types', () => {
            class TestClass {}
            expect(TestClass.is.type()).toBe(true);
            expect(func.is.type()).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('null and undefined', () => {
        it('should handle null checks through Object prototype', () => {
            const nullValue = null;
            expect(() => nullValue.is.null()).toThrow();  // can't access .is on null
            expect(() => nullValue.is.undefined()).toThrow();
        });

        it('should handle undefined checks through Object prototype', () => {
            const undefinedValue = undefined;
            expect(() => undefinedValue.is.undefined()).toThrow();  // can't access .is on undefined

        });
    });

    describe('specified/unspecified', () => {

            expect("test".is.specified()).toBe(true);
            expect(42..is.specified()).toBe(true);
            expect(true.is.specified()).toBe(true);
        });

        it('should handle edge cases', () => {
            expect(0..is.specified()).toBe(true);
            expect("".is.specified()).toBe(true);
            expect(false.is.specified()).toBe(true);
        });

            expect(() => 42..is.string({ orThrow: true })).toThrow();
            expect(() => true.is.object({ orThrow: true })).toThrow();
            expect(() => [].is.string({ orThrow: true })).toThrow();
        });

        it('should use custom error messages', () => {
            const customMsg = "Custom error message";
            expect(() => "test".is.number({ orThrow: customMsg })).toThrow(customMsg);
            expect(() => 42..is.string({ orThrow: customMsg })).toThrow(customMsg);

export class Is<T = any> extends Function {
    constructor(private value: T) {
        super();
        return new Proxy(this, {
            apply: (target, thisArg, args) => (instanceIs as Function)(this.value, ...args),
            get: (target, prop) => {
                return (this as any)[prop];
            },
        });
    }

    get undefined(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.undefined(this.value);
    }

    get null(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.null(this.value);
    }

    get string(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.string(this.value);
    }

    get number(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.number(this.value);
    }

    get boolean(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.boolean(this.value);
    }

    get bigint(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.bigint(this.value);
    }

    get symbol(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.symbol(this.value);
    }

    get object(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.object(this.value);
    }

    get function(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.function(this.value);
    }

    get type(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.type(this.value);
    }

    get emptyObject(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.emptyObject(this.value);
    }

    get populatedObject(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.populatedObject(this.value);
    }

    get array(): boolean {

    }

    get emptyArray(): boolean {

    }

    get populatedArray(): boolean {

    }

    get specified(): boolean {

    }

    get unspecified(): boolean {

    }

    get positiveInfinity(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.positiveInfinity(this.value);
    }

    get negativeInfinity(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.negativeInfinity(this.value);
    }

    get nan(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.nan(this.value as number);
    }

    get notNan(): boolean {
        return instanceIs.notNan(this.value as number);
    }

    // Methods that need parameters
    equal(other: any): boolean {
        return instanceIs.equal(this.value, other);
    }

    parentType(parentType: Constructor): boolean {
        return instanceIs.parentType(this.value, parentType);
    }

    childType(childType: Constructor): boolean {
        return instanceIs.childType(this.value, childType);

    instanceOf<U>(type: Constructor<U>): boolean {
        return instanceIs.instanceOf(this.value, type);
    }
}

export class MustBe<T = any> extends Function {
    private static formatMessage(message?: string): string {
        if (!message) return message;
        
        // Strip "because" prefix and capitalize next letter
        return message.replace(/^because[:\s]?\s*/i, (match) => {
            const restOfMessage = message.slice(match.length);
            return restOfMessage.charAt(0).toUpperCase() + restOfMessage.slice(1);
        });
    }

    constructor(private value: T) {
        super();
        return new Proxy(this, {
            apply: (target, thisArg, args) => {
                const [type, message] = args;
                if (!instanceIs(this.value, type)) {
                    throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || `Value must be instance of ${type.name}`);
                }
                return this.value;
            },
            get: (target, prop) => {
                return (this as any)[prop];
            },
        });
    }

    undefined(message?: string): asserts value is undefined {
        if (!instanceIs.undefined(this.value)) {
            throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || "Value must be undefined");
        }
    }

    null(message?: string): asserts value is null {
        if (!instanceIs.null(this.value)) {
            throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || "Value must be null");
        }
    }

    string(message?: string): asserts value is string {
        if (!instanceIs.string(this.value)) {
            throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || "Value must be a string");
        }
    }

    number(message?: string): asserts value is number {
        if (!instanceIs.number(this.value)) {
            throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || "Value must be a number");
        }
    }

    boolean(message?: string): asserts value is boolean {
        if (!instanceIs.boolean(this.value)) {
            throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || "Value must be a boolean");
        }
    }

    bigint(message?: string): asserts value is BigInt {
        if (!instanceIs.bigint(this.value)) {
            throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || "Value must be a bigint");
        }
    }

    symbol(message?: string): asserts value is Symbol {
        if (!instanceIs.symbol(this.value)) {
            throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || "Value must be a symbol");
        }
    }

    object(message?: string): asserts value is object {
        if (!instanceIs.object(this.value)) {
            throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || "Value must be an object");
        }
    }

    // ... continue with other assertions ...

    equal(other: any, message?: string): asserts value is typeof other {
        if (!instanceIs.equal(this.value, other)) {
            throw new Error(MustBe.formatMessage(message) || `Value must be equal to ${other}`);
        }
    }
}

// Usage examples:
// x.is(String)              // returns boolean
// x.is.string               // returns boolean
// x.mustBe(String)          // throws if not String
// x.mustBe.string()         // throws if not string
// x.mustBe.string("because: needs to be text")  // throws with formatted message

describe('Is Property', () => {
    describe('String values', () => {
        const str = "test string";
        
        it('identifies strings through properties', () => {
            expect(str.is.string).toBe(true);
            expect(str.is.number).toBe(false);
            expect(str.is.boolean).toBe(false);
            expect(str.is.undefined).toBe(false);
            expect(str.is.null).toBe(false);
            expect(str.is.object).toBe(false);
        });

        it('works with equality', () => {
            expect(str.is.equal("test string")).toBe(true);
            expect(str.is.equal("different")).toBe(false);
        });

        it('works as a function', () => {
            expect(str.is(String)).toBe(true);
            expect(str.is(Number)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('Number values', () => {
        const num = 42;
        const nan = NaN;
        const posInf = Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY;
        const negInf = Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY;

        it('identifies numbers through properties', () => {
            expect(num.is.number).toBe(true);
            expect(num.is.string).toBe(false);
            expect(num.is.notNan).toBe(true);
            expect(num.is.nan).toBe(false);
        });

        it('handles special number values', () => {
            expect(nan.is.nan).toBe(true);
            expect(nan.is.notNan).toBe(false);
            expect(posInf.is.positiveInfinity).toBe(true);
            expect(negInf.is.negativeInfinity).toBe(true);
        });

        it('works as a function', () => {
            expect(num.is(Number)).toBe(true);
            expect(num.is(String)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('Boolean values', () => {
        const bool = true;

        it('identifies booleans through properties', () => {
            expect(bool.is.boolean).toBe(true);
            expect(bool.is.string).toBe(false);
            expect(bool.is.number).toBe(false);
        });

        it('works as a function', () => {
            expect(bool.is(Boolean)).toBe(true);
            expect(bool.is(Number)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('Object values', () => {
        const emptyObj = {};
        const populatedObj = { key: 'value' };

        it('identifies objects through properties', () => {
            expect(emptyObj.is.object).toBe(true);
            expect(emptyObj.is.emptyObject).toBe(true);
            expect(emptyObj.is.populatedObject).toBe(false);
            
            expect(populatedObj.is.object).toBe(true);
            expect(populatedObj.is.emptyObject).toBe(false);
            expect(populatedObj.is.populatedObject).toBe(true);
        });

        it('works with inheritance checks', () => {
            class Parent {}
            class Child extends Parent {}
            
            const parent = new Parent();
            const child = new Child();

            expect(Child.is.childType(Parent)).toBe(true);
            expect(Parent.is.parentType(Child)).toBe(true);
            expect(child.is.instanceOf(Parent)).toBe(true);
            expect(parent.is.instanceOf(Child)).toBe(false);
        });

        it('works as a function', () => {
            expect(emptyObj.is(Object)).toBe(true);
            expect(emptyObj.is(Array)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('Array values', () => {
        const emptyArr: any[] = [];
        const populatedArr = [1, 2, 3];

        it('identifies arrays through properties', () => {
            expect(emptyArr.is.array).toBe(true);
            expect(emptyArr.is.emptyArray).toBe(true);
            expect(emptyArr.is.populatedArray).toBe(false);
            
            expect(populatedArr.is.array).toBe(true);
            expect(populatedArr.is.emptyArray).toBe(false);
            expect(populatedArr.is.populatedArray).toBe(true);
        });

        it('works as a function', () => {
            expect(emptyArr.is(Array)).toBe(true);
            expect(emptyArr.is(Object)).toBe(true); // arrays are objects
        });
    });

    describe('Symbol values', () => {
        const sym = Symbol('test');

        it('identifies symbols through properties', () => {
            expect(sym.is.symbol).toBe(true);
            expect(sym.is.string).toBe(false);
            expect(sym.is.number).toBe(false);
        });

        it('works as a function', () => {
            expect(sym.is(Symbol)).toBe(true);
            expect(sym.is(String)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('BigInt values', () => {
        const bigInt = BigInt(42);

        it('identifies bigints through properties', () => {
            expect(bigInt.is.bigint).toBe(true);
            expect(bigInt.is.number).toBe(false);
            expect(bigInt.is.string).toBe(false);
        });

        it('works as a function', () => {
            expect(bigInt.is(BigInt)).toBe(true);
            expect(bigInt.is(Number)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('Function values', () => {
        const func = () => {};
        class TestClass {}

        it('identifies functions through properties', () => {
            expect(func.is.function).toBe(true);
            expect(func.is.string).toBe(false);
        });

        it('identifies constructor functions correctly', () => {
            expect(TestClass.is.type).toBe(true);
            expect(func.is.type).toBe(false);
        });

        it('works as a function', () => {
            expect(func.is(Function)).toBe(true);
            expect(func.is(String)).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('null and undefined', () => {
        // Note: Can't test directly as .is won't exist on null/undefined
        const obj = {};
        it('identifies null and undefined through properties when available', () => {
            expect(obj.is.null).toBe(false);
            expect(obj.is.undefined).toBe(false);
        });
    });

    describe('specified/unspecified values', () => {
        const specified = "value";
        const zero = 0;
        const emptyString = "";
        const falseValue = false;

        it('correctly identifies specified values', () => {
            expect(specified.is.specified).toBe(true);
            expect(specified.is.unspecified).toBe(false);
            
            // Edge cases that should be specified
            expect(zero.is.specified).toBe(true);
            expect(emptyString.is.specified).toBe(true);
            expect(falseValue.is.specified).toBe(true);
        });
    });
});

    // Function behavior
    describe('function call behavior', () => {
        it('works as a function for type checking', () => {
            expect("string".is(String)).toBe(true);
            expect((42).is(Number)).toBe(true);
            expect(true.is(Boolean)).toBe(true);
            expect([].is(Array)).toBe(true);
            expect(({}).is(Object)).toBe(true);
        });

        it('returns false for incorrect types', () => {
            expect("string".is(Number)).toBe(false);
            expect((42).is(String)).toBe(false);
            expect(true.is(Array)).toBe(false);
            expect([].is(String)).toBe(false);
        });

        it('works with inheritance', () => {
            class Parent {}
            class Child extends Parent {}
            const child = new Child();
            
            expect(child.is(Child)).toBe(true);
            expect(child.is(Parent)).toBe(true);
            expect(child.is(Object)).toBe(true);
        });

        it('works with built-in inheritance', () => {
            const arr = [];
            expect(arr.is(Array)).toBe(true);
            expect(arr.is(Object)).toBe(true);
        });
    });

    // Edge cases and special scenarios
    describe('edge cases', () => {
        it('handles NaN correctly', () => {
            expect(NaN.is.number).toBe(true);
            expect(NaN.is.nan).toBe(true);
            expect(NaN.is.notNan).toBe(false);
        });

        it('handles zero correctly', () => {
            expect((0).is.number).toBe(true);
            expect((0).is.specified).toBe(true);
            expect((0).is.notNan).toBe(true);
        });

        it('handles empty string correctly', () => {
            expect("".is.string).toBe(true);
            expect("".is.specified).toBe(true);
            expect("".is.emptyArray).toBe(false);
        });

        it('handles false correctly', () => {
            expect(false.is.boolean).toBe(true);
            expect(false.is.specified).toBe(true);
            expect(false.is.undefined).toBe(false);
        });

        it('handles boxed primitives correctly', () => {
            expect(new String("test").is.string).toBe(true);
            expect(new Number(42).is.number).toBe(true);
            expect(new Boolean(true).is.boolean).toBe(true);
        });

        it('handles symbol registration correctly', () => {
            const sym1 = Symbol('test');
            const sym2 = Symbol('test');
            const sym3 = Symbol.for('test');
            const sym4 = Symbol.for('test');

            expect(sym1.is.equal(sym2)).toBe(false); // Different symbols
            expect(sym3.is.equal(sym4)).toBe(true);  // Same registered symbol
        });

        it('handles promise-like objects correctly', () => {
            const promise = Promise.resolve();
            expect(promise.is.instanceOf(Promise)).toBe(true);
            expect(promise.is.object).toBe(true);
            expect(({ then: () => {} }).is.instanceOf(Promise)).toBe(false);
        });

        it('handles array-like objects correctly', () => {
            const arrayLike = { length: 0 };
            expect(arrayLike.is.array).toBe(false);
            expect(arrayLike.is.object).toBe(true);
        });
    });

    // Multiple checks combinations
    describe('combined checks', () => {
        it('can combine multiple checks meaningfully', () => {
            const arr = [1, 2, 3];
            expect(arr.is.array && arr.is.populatedArray).toBe(true);
            expect(arr.is.array && arr.is.emptyArray).toBe(false);
        });

        it('can check type and properties together', () => {
            const str = "test";
            expect(str.is.string && str.is.specified).toBe(true);
            expect(str.is(String) && str.is.specified).toBe(true);
        });

        it('handles complex type hierarchies', () => {
            class A {}
            class B extends A {}
            class C extends B {}
            const c = new C();

            expect(c.is.instanceOf(C) && c.is.instanceOf(B) && c.is.instanceOf(A)).toBe(true);
            expect(C.is.childType(B) && B.is.childType(A)).toBe(true);
            expect(A.is.parentType(B) && B.is.parentType(C)).toBe(true);
        });
    });
});
